title: Telescopes

learn.summary: A telescope's most important spec is aperture — light-gathering diameter — not magnification; ignore any box advertising '600x power.' The best first scope by consensus is a 6-8 inch Dobsonian reflector: maximum aperture per dollar, no complexity. The real best telescope, as the saying goes, is the one you'll actually use.

do: Before buying anything, attend a local astronomy club star party and look through at least three different telescope types — clubs exist for exactly this.

children.title: Refractor, Reflector, Cat

learn.summary: Refractors bend light through lenses (rugged, sharp, expensive per inch), reflectors use mirrors per Newton's 1668 design (cheapest aperture, needs occasional alignment), and catadioptrics like Schmidt-Cassegrains fold long focal lengths into stubby portable tubes. A Dobsonian is just a Newtonian reflector on a brilliantly simple lazy-susan mount, popularized by John Dobson. Each design trades cost, portability, and maintenance differently.

do: Write down your honest constraints — budget, storage space, how far you must carry gear to a dark spot — and match them to one telescope type before browsing any store.

children.title: Mounts

learn.summary: Alt-azimuth mounts move up/down and left/right — intuitive and ideal for visual observing. Equatorial mounts tilt one axis parallel to Earth's, so a single slow motion cancels sky rotation — essential for astrophotography, overkill for beginners. A wobbly mount ruins a great tube; seasoned buyers put as much budget into the mount as the optics.

do: At a store or star party, tap the tube of a mounted telescope lightly and time how long the view takes to stop shaking — over 2 seconds means the mount is undersized.

children.title: Eyepieces & Magnification

learn.summary: Magnification = telescope focal length divided by eyepiece focal length, so a 1200mm scope with a 10mm eyepiece gives 120x. Useful maximum is about 50x per inch of aperture; past that you magnify blur. Low power (30-50x) is for finding and rich fields, medium (100x) for the Moon and clusters, high (150-250x) for planets on steady nights.

do: Compute the magnification of every eyepiece you (or a friend's scope) have, and label each one low/medium/high for quick selection in the dark.

children.title: First Light Routine

learn.summary: 'First light' is a new scope's first real observation — and it goes best with a plan: align the finder in daylight on a distant chimney, start on the Moon or a bright planet, and use your lowest-power eyepiece for everything until aiming feels natural. Let the scope cool outdoors for 30-60 minutes first; a warm mirror boils the image. Failure to align the finder is the number one cause of frustrated returns.

do: Write a five-step first-light checklist (cool-down, finder alignment, low-power eyepiece, easy target, log entry) and keep it with the scope — use it even if 'the scope' is borrowed.

children.title: Collimation & Care

learn.summary: Reflectors need periodic collimation — aligning the mirrors so light focuses precisely — checked with a collimation cap or laser in a few minutes once learned. Miscollimation is the top reason 'my telescope is blurry.' Never touch or over-clean optics: a little dust harms nothing, while aggressive cleaning scratches coatings permanently.

do: If you have a reflector, do the star test: center a bright star, defocus slightly, and check whether the shadow of the secondary mirror sits dead-center in the donut.
